caption: Yellow swimming sea cucumber (Enypniastes eximia) covered in hydroids seen just before the remotely operated vehicles reached the seafloor on the Kaʻena Slope during Dive 08 of the 2025 ROV and Mapping Shakedown expedition.
Whiplash Squid: September 3, 2019. Seen while exploring Kinlan Canyon, off the coast of Rhode Island, at 1,030 meters (3,380 feet) depth.

credit: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration
caption: An exciting observation made during the 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration expedition was two of these jellyfish that measured nearly 30 centimeters (11.8 inches) across. Scientists identified the jellyfish as belonging to the genus Tiburonia (likely T. granrojo). The white balls seen on the subumbrella (the concave undersurface) of the jellies may be brooded juveniles; while it has been suspected that this genus does brood its young, this had not been confirmed, making these observations potentially even more impressive than just the size of the jellies! Video courtesy of NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration.

credit: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2025 ROV and Mapping Shakedown (EX2502)
caption: Pyrosome seen while exploring Penguin Bank during Dive 04 of the 2025 ROV and Mapping Shakedown expedition.

credit: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Windows to the Deep 2019
caption: below its body, this adorable bobtail squid was seen at a depth of 552 meters (1,811 feet) in Baltimore Canyon on the Mid-Atlantic continental shelf during the Windows to the Deep 2019: Exploration of the Deep-Sea Habitats of the Southeast United States expedition. These cephalopods are small, generally no bigger than a golf ball, and despite their common name, they aren’t actually squids. credit: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Deep-Sea Symphony: Exploring the Musicians Seamounts
caption: Siphonophore Tangled mass of string floating along in the ocean? Nope. It's a siphonophore! And if the fact that it is alive isn't weird enough, consider this: It's not one individual animal, but a whole bunch working together as a single colony. Talk about teamwork! Seen exploring at a depth of approximately 800 meters (2,625 feet) off of Hawaii during the Deep-Sea Symphony: Exploring the Musicians Seamounts expedition.

credit: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2019 Southeastern U.S. Deep-Sea Exploration
caption: Schaefer’s Anglerfish This goosefish ( Sladenia shaefersi ) has the common name of Schaefer's anglerfish. While we do encounter anglerfish in our deep-ocean exploration, this particular species is not as well known, so catching a glimpse of it and its modified fins that act much like feet, allowing it to "walk" on the seafloor, during Dive 12 of the 2019 Southeastern U.S. Deep-sea Exploration was indeed a treat.

credit: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Deep-Sea Symphony: Exploring the Musicians Seamounts
caption: This fangtooth spent some time examining remotely operated vehicle Deep Discoverer at a depth of 800 meters (2,600 feet) during NOAA Ocean Exploration’s 2017 expedition “Deep-Sea Symphony: Exploring the Musicians Seamounts.”

credit: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration
caption: During the third dive of the 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration expedition we saw several tripod fish standing on their fins on the seafloor. These fish face into the current and use their long appendages to sense food as it drifts by in the water column.
